title: Spending money
summary: Choose between the present perfect and the past simple. Talk about money.

blocks.h: Present perfect: have / has + past participle
blocks.p: Use the present perfect when the time is not important or not finished: experiences in your life (often with ever / never), and recent actions with a result now (often with just).
ex: Have you ever forgotten your PIN?
I've never had a credit card.
Oh no! I've just dropped my phone in the sink.

blocks.p: already (= sooner than expected) goes before the main verb in positive sentences. yet goes at the end of negatives and questions.
ex: I've already booked the tickets.
The bank hasn't answered my email yet.
Have you opened your new account yet?

blocks.p: Use the past simple when you say or ask when something happened, or the time is clearly finished: yesterday, last year, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child.
ex: I bought these boots in the sales last January.
When did you open your bank account?
We didn't go on holiday last year.

blocks.p: We often start with the present perfect (the general experience) and continue with the past simple (the details).
ex: Have you ever been to Japan? Yes, I have. I went there in 2018.
I've lost my keys. I left them on the bus this morning.

items: take money from someone and give it back later (borrow FROM)
give money to someone for a time (lend TO)
need to pay back money you borrowed: I owe you €20
spend money badly, on useless things
don't have enough money to buy something
ask a price for a service: They charged me €60
have a price: These shoes cost $200
have a certain value: My car is worth €5,000
receive money or property from someone who has died
put money into a business or property to make a profit
collect money for a good cause
a paper that shows how much you must pay
the money you have and your plan for spending it
paying by holding your card or phone near a reader
you pay a company and they pay if something bad happens
money that you borrow from a bank
a loan to buy a house or flat
the money you get every month for your job
money that you pay to the government
Can I pay by card? / I'll pay in cash.
I spend too much on clothes.
I never lend money to friends.

blocks.p: The letter o has several sounds. The most common are /ɒ/ (short), /əʊ/ (like 'go') and /ʌ/ (like 'up').
ex: money
honest
loan

blocks.p: When or is stressed it's usually /ɔː/: afford, mortgage, order. But after w it's usually /ɜː/: work, worth, world.
ex: afford
mortgage
worth
work

grammar.q: Oh no! I ___ my finger!

grammar.q: When ___ your first car?

grammar.e: yet at the end of negatives.

grammar.e: Details with a finished time → past simple.

title: Changing lives
summary: Say how long something has lasted with for / since. Use strong adjectives.

sections.title: Present perfect + for / since; present perfect continuous

blocks.p: To talk about a situation that started in the past and continues now, use the present perfect, not the present simple. Use for + a period of time and since + a point in time.
ex: I've had this bike for six years.
My aunt has lived in Cork since 2015.
How long have you lived here?

blocks.p: for: two weeks, ten years, a long time, ages. since: Monday, 2010, June, I was a child, last summer.
ex: for three months
since last Christmas
since I was at university

blocks.h: Present perfect continuous: have / has been + verb-ing
blocks.p: With action verbs we often use the present perfect continuous with for / since / How long to emphasize the activity continuing up to now. With non-action verbs (know, have = possess, be, like) use the present perfect simple.
ex: How long have you been saving for the trip?
The baby has been crying since six o'clock.
We've known each other since primary school.

blocks.h: Recent activities with a present result
blocks.p: We also use the continuous for an activity that has just stopped and explains what we see now.
ex: You're out of breath. Have you been running?
Yes, I've been jogging in the park.

blocks.p: With live and work both forms are fine with for / since.
ex: I've worked here since 2019.
I've been working here since 2019.

groups.note: Strong adjectives already mean 'very ___'. Use absolutely or really with them, NOT very: absolutely exhausted, NOT very exhausted.

blocks.p: In questions with How long have you been…?, the important words are stressed and have you been is said very fast: /əv jə bɪn/.
ex: How long have you been studying?
How long have you known her?

blocks.p: We often give strong adjectives extra stress to show emotion.
ex: I'm absolutely exhausted!
The water was freezing!
I'm starving!

grammar.q: I ___ here since 2018.
grammar.e: Started in the past and continues → present perfect, not present simple.

grammar.q: I've had this laptop ___ three years.
He's been in hospital ___ Monday.
How long ___ your best friend?
grammar.e: know is non-action → present perfect simple.

grammar.q: It ___ all day. Take an umbrella.
grammar.e: Action continuing up to now → present perfect continuous.

grammar.q: Why are you so dirty? What ___?
grammar.e: Recent activity with a visible result.

grammar.q: I ___ her since we were children.
How long have you ___ (wait) for the bus? Use the continuous.
My neighbours ___ (argue) for an hour. I can't sleep! Use the continuous.
Complete with for or since: I haven't seen him ___ ages.
Complete with for or since: My dad has worked for the same company ___ he left university.
grammar.e: since + a point in time (a clause).

vocabulary.e: absolutely + strong adjective; very + normal adjective.

vocabulary.q: A: Are you scared of flying? B: I'm ___! I never fly.

pronunciation.q: In 'How long have you been waiting?', which words are stressed?
pronunciation.e: Content words are stressed; have you been is fast and weak.
